deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is a single aphoristic remark in Hilbert's hand, closed off by a short horizontal rule. The rest of the page is blank apart from faint bleed-through from the reverse side.

Translation: "One can really think of only ONE law of nature! The various individual parts cannot be separated from one another at all, e.g. the law of electricity, the magnetic [law], the law of gravitation!" The word "ein" is underlined for emphasis.

Content: this is a statement of a unity-of-physics programme. Electrostatics, magnetism and gravitation are not independent laws but aspects of one law of nature.

Context: the previous page ends a remark about electrodynamics and relativity theory and has a jab at Kronecker. The next page continues with philosophical and foundational aphorisms: Kant's antinomies as calculation errors in the logical calculus, axiomatizability as the criterion of science, and consistency of the axiom of choice. So this folio belongs to a sequence of loose philosophical notes, not a technical calculation.

The remark echoes Hilbert's 1915–16 'Die Grundlagen der Physik'. There, building on Mie's electrodynamics and Einstein's gravitation, he sought a single variational principle from which both the gravitational and the electromagnetic field equations follow. He framed this as a unified theory of all physical phenomena.

results.what: Programmatic claim that there is only one law of nature, of which the electric, magnetic and gravitational laws are inseparable parts
results.modern_name: Unified field theory / unification of the fundamental interactions (philosophical statement)
results.usually_credited_to: Mie (1912–13), Hilbert (1915–16, 'Die Grundlagen der Physik'), later Weyl (1918), Kaluza (1921), Einstein's unified field theory programme

deep.surprise_reason: A purely philosophical aphorism. Hilbert's belief in a single unified physical law (gravitation plus electromagnetism) is well documented in his 1915–16 papers and lectures. The note adds only a private, emphatic formulation of a known position.
transcription_corrections: 'ein' in the first line is underlined in the manuscript (emphasis: 'nur EIN Naturgesetz').

The struck-out fragment before 'magnetische' looks like 'de' or 'da' (probably the start of 'das'), crossed through. The intended reading is 'Elektricitätsgesetz, das magnetische, Gravitationsgesetz'.
The struck-out ending of 'Gravitationsgesetz' looks like scribbled-over 'e' plus a stroke (an aborted plural 'Gravitationsgesetze'), consistent with the given '[-e-]'.
'Elektricitätsgesetz' is written in old orthography with 'c'; the abbreviation 'z. B.' is written as 'z. B.' (the second letter looks like a cursive B).
The faint marks in the lower part of the page are bleed-through from the reverse side and are not text of this folio.
